questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What makes an oscillation simple harmonic
questions.learningObjective: identify the feature of the restoring force that defines simple harmonic motion
questions.stem: A body oscillates back and forth about a point of equilibrium. What makes that oscillation simple harmonic rather than merely periodic?

options.text: The restoring force is constant in size, so the body moves with a uniform acceleration
options.misconception: believes a constant restoring force produces simple harmonic motion

options.text: The restoring force is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium, and always points back towards it
The restoring force is proportional to the square of the displacement from equilibrium
options.misconception: believes the restoring force goes as the square of the displacement

options.text: The period of the motion is the same however large the starting displacement is
options.misconception: treats amplitude independence as the defining feature rather than a consequence

questions.explanation: Simple harmonic motion is defined by the shape of the restoring force and by nothing else. The force must be proportional to the displacement and directed towards the equilibrium point, so writing it as minus a constant times the displacement gives an acceleration of that same form, and that single statement is what produces a sinusoidal displacement with a period independent of amplitude. A constant restoring force, which is the second option, produces uniform acceleration instead, and the body simply reverses and leaves, it does not oscillate at all. A force going as the square of the displacement, the third option, does produce an oscillation but the period then depends on how far the body is displaced, so the motion is periodic without being simple harmonic. The amplitude independence quoted in the fourth option is a genuine result of the correct rule, but quoting a consequence of the definition in place of the definition is how a pendulum and a bouncing ball end up confused with each other.
questions.hint: The defining statement is about the force, not about the motion or the period.

questions.topic: Spring constant recovered from a force and its extension
questions.learningObjective: recover a spring constant from a single force and extension pair
questions.stem: A spring is found to need a pull of 3.60 N to stretch it 0.0450 m beyond its natural length, and the pull is proportional to the extension at all lengths. What is the spring constant in N per metre?

Reading it off a table of measurements instead of a single pair gives the same figure, because the force and extension pairs all sit on a straight line through the origin: the slope of the first segment is 80.0 N per metre, of the second 80.0 N per metre, and of the third 80.0 N per metre, all of them 80.0 to the accuracy of the table. The units are worth stating, since the constant is what converts an extension in metres into a force in newtons, and a spring with a constant of 80.0 N per metre supplies 8.00 N when stretched 0.1000 m, which is a useful check that the number behaves like a stiffness rather than like a force.
questions.hint: The spring constant is the force per unit extension.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Period of a mass on a horizontal spring
questions.learningObjective: compute the period of a mass-spring oscillator
questions.stem: A mass of 0.400 kg is attached to a spring of spring constant 160 N per metre and oscillates without friction. Taking the period of a mass on a spring as two pi times the square root of the mass divided by the spring constant, what is the period in seconds?
questions.explanation: The period is two pi times the square root of the mass divided by the spring constant, and the ratio here is 0.400 divided by 160, which is 0.00250 in units of seconds squared. Its square root is 0.0500 s, and multiplying by two pi gives 0.314 s. The same number comes from the angular frequency rather than the period, since the angular frequency of a mass on a spring is the square root of the spring constant divided by the mass, 20.0 rad per second, and the period is two pi divided by that, which is 0.314 s. A useful structural check is that the mass and the spring constant enter only as a ratio, so quadrupling the mass doubles the period while doubling the spring constant multiplies the period by one over the square root of two, and neither change alters the shape of the motion, which remains sinusoidal whatever the period turns out to be.
questions.hint: Period is two pi times the square root of mass divided by spring constant.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Speed of a mass-spring oscillator passing through equilibrium
questions.learningObjective: obtain the equilibrium speed of an oscillator from its amplitude and frequency
questions.stem: An oscillator consists of a mass of 0.400 kg on a spring of spring constant 160 N per metre, displaced 0.0500 m from equilibrium and released. What is its speed in m per second as it passes through the equilibrium position?
questions.explanation: All of the energy is stored as elastic energy at the turning point, and none of it is kinetic, so the energy is one half of the spring constant times the square of the amplitude, 0.200 J. At the equilibrium position all of that has become kinetic energy, one half of the mass times the square of the speed, and equating the two gives a speed of the amplitude times the square root of the spring constant divided by the mass, which is 0.0500 times 20.0, that is 1.000 m per second. The acceleration amplitude provides an independent route: the greatest acceleration is the acceleration amplitude, 20.0 m per second squared, and the speed at the centre follows from the fact that the acceleration there is the greatest, so equating the kinetic energy to one half of the mass times that acceleration times the distance from the turning point, which is half the amplitude, gives 1.000 m per second. The two routes agree, and both show why the amplitude enters directly: an oscillator driven twice as far moves twice as fast at the centre.
questions.hint: Conserve energy from the turning point to the equilibrium point.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Period of a simple pendulum at small angles
questions.learningObjective: compute the small-angle period of a simple pendulum
questions.stem: A simple pendulum consists of a small bob on a massless string of length 0.900 m, swinging in a vertical plane with an amplitude small enough that the small-angle rule applies. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared, what is its period in seconds?
questions.explanation: The small-angle period of a simple pendulum is two pi times the square root of the length divided by the acceleration due to gravity, so the ratio is 0.900 divided by 9.80, which is 0.0918 in units of seconds squared, its square root is 0.303 s, and the period is 1.90 s. Taking the angular frequency first gives the same answer by a different route: the angular frequency of a small-angle pendulum is the square root of the acceleration due to gravity divided by the length, 3.30 rad per second, and the period is two pi divided by that, 1.90 s. The structure of the result is what makes pendulums useful in clocks, because the length appears under a square root and is the only thing that matters, so lengthening the pendulum by a factor of four doubles the period and therefore halves the rate at which a clock using it ticks. The small-angle qualification is the real limitation, since a swing of twenty degrees already lengthens the period by rather more than the small-angle error at five degrees would suggest.
questions.hint: Period is two pi times the square root of length divided by the acceleration due to gravity.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why the pendulum period does not depend on the bob mass
questions.learningObjective: explain the cancellation of the bob mass in the pendulum period
questions.stem: Two simple pendulums have the same length of 0.900 m but bobs of very different mass, 0.0200 kg and 2.00 kg. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared, do they swing with the same period, and why?

options.text: No, because the heavier bob stretches the string and lengthens the pendulum
options.misconception: believes the weight of the bob stretches the string enough to change the period

options.text: No, because a heavier bob needs more force to accelerate and so swings more slowly
options.misconception: applies the fixed-force reasoning of a linear oscillator to a pendulum

options.text: Yes, because the restoring force scales with the mass and so does the inertia, and the two cancel exactly
Yes, because the period of any oscillator depends only on its length
options.misconception: believes length is the only property that ever sets a period

questions.explanation: The bob is subject to two forces, its weight and the tension in the string, and dividing the tangential equation of motion by the mass removes the bob from it entirely. Concretely, the restoring torque is the weight times the horizontal offset of the bob, and the moment of inertia of a point bob about the pivot is the mass times the square of the length, so the mass appears once in the numerator of the acceleration and once in the denominator of the inertia, and the two cancel. Both pendulums therefore have the period two pi times the square root of 0.900 divided by 9.80, which is 1.90 s, and a factor of 100.0 in the mass makes no difference at all. The fourth option states something true about this pair and nothing in general, since the length is not the only thing that sets a period, and the first two options confuse this with other situations: a heavier bob does not stretch a string appreciably, and the mass-independence is a cancellation rather than an absence of the mass from the physics.
questions.hint: Write the equation of motion for the bob and divide through by the mass.

questions.topic: Two springs in series behaving as one softer spring
questions.learningObjective: combine spring constants in series from the added extensions
questions.stem: Two springs of spring constants 160 N per metre and 0.1000 N per metre are joined end to end in series and a mass of 0.400 kg hangs from the joint. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared, what is the effective spring constant of the combination in N per metre, and how far does the mass stretch it in total?
questions.explanation: In series the same pull acts through both springs, and the total extension is the sum of the two extensions each spring would make on its own. Writing the extension of the pair as the weight divided by the unknown effective constant and also as the weight divided by each spring in turn, the reciprocals add, so the effective constant is the one divided by the sum of the reciprocals. Here that is the one divided by the sum of 0.00625 and 10.00, giving 0.0999 N per metre. Working with extensions rather than constants confirms it: the weight is 3.92 N, the softer spring stretches 0.0245 m and the stiffer one 39.2 m, a total of 39.2 m, and dividing the weight by that extension returns 0.0999 N per metre. The physical reading is that springs in series are always softer than either spring alone, so the period of the oscillator lengthens, while springs in parallel are always stiffer and the period shortens.
questions.hint: In series the pull is the same through both springs, so the extensions add and the reciprocals of the constants add.

questions.topic: Two springs in parallel behaving as one stiffer spring
questions.learningObjective: combine spring constants in parallel from the shared extension
questions.stem: Two springs of spring constants 160 N per metre and 240 N per metre are joined side by side in parallel, both attached to the same rigid bar, and a mass of 0.400 kg hangs from the bar. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared, what is the effective spring constant of the pair in N per metre, and what is the extension of each spring?
questions.explanation: In parallel both springs are stretched by the same amount, and each contributes its own share of the total pull, so the pulls add at a common extension and the constants add directly. That gives 160 plus 240, which is 400 N per metre. Deriving it from the extension instead of adding the constants gives the same result: the weight is 3.92 N, the pair stretches by the weight divided by the total constant, which is 0.00980 m, and dividing the weight by that extension returns 400 N per metre. Each spring carries the share of the pull that matches its own stiffness, so the softer one takes 0.400 of the total and the stiffer one 0.600, while both stretch by the identical 0.00980 m. The practical contrast with the series case is the whole point: parallel springs give a stiffer system and therefore a shorter period, and they are the arrangement used when a load must be shared without the springs moving relative to one another.

questions.topic: Shift of equilibrium when a spring is hung vertically
questions.learningObjective: find the new equilibrium of a vertical spring and confirm the period is unchanged
questions.stem: A spring of spring constant 160 N per metre hangs vertically and a mass of 0.400 kg is attached to its lower end. questions.topic: Total energy stored in a mass-spring oscillator

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Period of a torsional pendulum
questions.learningObjective: compute the period of a torsional oscillator from its moment of inertia and stiffness
questions.stem: A torsion wire resists twisting with a restoring torque of 7.90e-5 N*m per radian, so a twist of one radian calls for a torque of that size, and a light disc of moment of inertia 2.00e-6 kg*m^2 is attached to it. What is the period in seconds of the resulting small torsional oscillation?
questions.explanation: A torsional oscillator obeys exactly the pattern of a mass on a spring, with the moment of inertia replacing the mass and the torsional stiffness replacing the spring constant. The period is therefore two pi times the square root of the moment of inertia divided by the stiffness, and here the ratio is 2.00e-6 divided by 7.90e-5, which is 0.0253 in units of seconds squared, giving 1.000 s. Taking the angular frequency first gives the same value, since the angular frequency of a torsional oscillator is the square root of the stiffness divided by the moment of inertia, 6.28 rad per second, and the period is two pi over that, 1.000 s. What makes torsional oscillators useful is that the restoring stiffness is set by the wire rather than by the moving mass, so the period is almost independent of what is attached, which is how a watch balance wheel keeps time despite changes in its own inertia as it warms up, and how a torsion balance can measure a force too small to hang on a spring.
questions.hint: The period is two pi times the square root of moment of inertia divided by torsional stiffness.

questions.topic: Energy of a pendulum at a finite swing angle
questions.learningObjective: compute the gravitational energy of a pendulum at a given angle
questions.stem: A pendulum bob of mass 0.0500 kg hangs on a massless string of length 1.20 m and is raised to an angle of 5.16 degrees from the downward vertical. For small angles the same energy is more simply one half of the weight times the length times the square of the angle, since one minus the cosine of a small angle is half its square, and that gives 0.00238 J, agreeing with the exact figure to within the small-angle error at this angle. The check worth keeping in mind is that the small-angle form understates the height, because the exact cosine makes the rise slightly less than half the square, and the difference grows as the square of the angle, so the approximation is trustworthy only in the small swings that the small-angle period already assumes.
questions.hint: The rise is the string length times one minus the cosine of the angle.

questions.topic: Dependence of the pendulum period on amplitude
questions.learningObjective: assess how far the pendulum period departs from its small-angle value at a finite angle
questions.stem: A pendulum of length 0.900 m is timed by counting many swings, and the measurement gives 1.90 s to three figures. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared and the swing amplitude as 5.00 degrees, what is the leading amplitude correction as a fraction of the small-angle period, and is the timing trustworthy?

options.text: The correction is about 0.00240, so the small-angle period understates it by a noticeable amount
options.misconception: overstates the amplitude correction by a factor of ten

options.text: The correction is exactly zero at any angle, since the period of a pendulum never depends on amplitude
options.misconception: believes the small-angle result is exact for every amplitude

options.text: The correction is proportional to the amplitude itself, so halving the swing halves the error
options.misconception: believes the correction scales linearly with the angle rather than with its square

options.text: The correction is about 2.4e-4, some 0.476 parts in a thousand, well below what the timing resolves

questions.explanation: The small-angle result is an approximation, and the leading error it carries grows with the square of the amplitude, with the period lengthening by one sixteenth of the square of the angle in radians. Here the angle is 5.00 degrees, which is 0.0873 rad, and its square is 0.00762, so the relative correction is one sixteenth of that, which is 4.76e-4. Multiplying the small-angle period of 1.90 s by one plus that gives 1.90 s, a change of about 0.906 milliseconds, and a timing that resolves only three significant figures over many swings is counting to far better than that. A swing reduced from ten degrees to five degrees cuts the error by a factor of four rather than a factor of two, which is why the fourth option is wrong even though it has the right sign, and why a seconds pendulum is specified with a small amplitude built into its design. The correct period also lengthens rather than shortens, because the finite swing spends its time further from the bottom where the restoring is weaker.

questions.topic: Oscillation of a liquid column in a U-tube
questions.learningObjective: compute the period of a liquid column oscillating in a U-tube
questions.stem: A U-tube of uniform bore is filled with a liquid of density 1.00e3 kg per cubic metre and oscillates without friction about its level position. The length of liquid in the tube is 0.800 m, measured along the tube from one open end to the other. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared, what is the period of the oscillation in seconds?
questions.explanation: If the liquid is displaced by a height x in one limb it rises by x in the other, so the difference in level is 2x and the net unbalanced weight of the displaced column is the cross-sectional area times 2x times the density times the acceleration due to gravity. Dividing by the volume of the whole column, the area times the length, the inertia that appears in the equation of motion is the mass times the length divided the area, and the acceleration equation becomes the acceleration proportional to minus 2x divided by the length times the acceleration due to gravity. That is a simple harmonic restoring acceleration, with the effective spring constant 2 times the density times the acceleration due to gravity divided by the length, so the period is two pi times the square root of the length divided by twice the acceleration due to gravity, which is 1.27 s. Going via the angular frequency, the square root of twice the acceleration due to gravity divided by the length, 4.95 rad per second, and then two pi over that, gives 1.27 s. The density cancels, which is the notable result: a mercury column of the same length oscillates at the same period as a water column, even though its mass and restoring force are thirteen and a half times larger.
questions.hint: The restoring force comes from the level difference, which is twice the displacement of either limb.

What is the angular frequency of the resulting damped oscillation in rad per second, and by what factor is it below the undamped value?

The natural angular frequency is the square root of the spring constant divided by the mass, 20.0 rad per second, and the damped angular frequency is that number in quadrature with half the damping constant, that is the square root of the square of the natural frequency less a quarter of the square of the damping constant. The sign of the shift is the physically interesting part: damping always lowers the frequency, which is why a struck bell that is heavily damped sounds flat compared with the same bell barely damped, and the limit of the formula is the point at which the quantity under the square root vanishes and the oscillation gives way to a pure decay, since beyond that there is no back-and-forth at all.

questions.topic: Effective length of a pendulum with a bob of finite size

questions.stem: A simple pendulum has a massless string of length 0.900 m carrying a uniform solid spherical bob of radius 0.0500 m and mass 0.200 kg. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared, what is the effective length of the pendulum in m, and what period in seconds does it swing with?
questions.explanation: A bob with size is not a point on the end of a string, and the size enters twice, through the distance of the bob's centre below the attachment point and through the bob's own tendency to rotate. The centre of the bob hangs 0.950 m below the pivot, and the moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere about a diameter is 2.00e-4 kg*m^2, which the parallel-axis theorem adds to the mass times the square of the centre distance to give 0.181 kg*m^2 about the pivot. The exact small-angle relation sets the angular frequency as the product of the acceleration due to gravity, the mass and the centre distance divided by the moment of inertia, and rewriting that in the point-mass form gives an effective length of the moment of inertia divided by the mass times the centre distance, which is 0.951 m. Splitting the same expression as the centre distance plus the bob's own inertia over the mass times that distance gives 0.951 m, the same value, and the resulting period is 1.96 s. The effective length is slightly longer than a point bob on a string of the same length would give, 1.90 s for the period, because the bob is held slightly below the attachment point.
questions.hint: Use the moment of inertia about the pivot and the distance to the bob centre, then divide one by the other through the mass.

questions.topic: Natural frequency of a spring oscillator stated as a frequency
questions.learningObjective: convert between the period and the frequency of an oscillator
questions.stem: A mass of 0.200 kg oscillates on a spring of spring constant 50.0 N per metre. What is the natural frequency of the oscillation in Hz, and what is the angular frequency in rad per second?
questions.explanation: The period of a mass on a spring is two pi times the square root of the mass divided by the spring constant, which is 0.397 s, and the frequency is its reciprocal, 2.52 Hz. The angular frequency is the same quantity expressed in radians per second rather than cycles per second, so it is the period multiplied by two pi, which is 15.8 rad per second, and equivalently the square root of the spring constant divided by the mass times that same two pi, giving 15.8 rad per second. Getting the factor of two pi right in each direction is the only real difficulty here, because the two conventions differ by exactly that factor and mixing them up gives an answer out by more than six. The physical content is the same in either convention: the frequency is set by the ratio of the stiffness to the mass, with the stiffness inside a square root, so doubling the mass lowers the frequency by a factor of the square root of two rather than by a factor of two.
questions.hint: Frequency is the reciprocal of the period; angular frequency is the period times two pi.

questions.topic: Density cancels from the period of a liquid column
questions.learningObjective: show that the liquid density cancels from the U-tube oscillation period
questions.stem: A U-tube of uniform bore is filled with mercury of density 1.36e4 kg per cubic metre and oscillates without friction, with 0.400 m of mercury in the tube measured along it from one open end to the other. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as 9.80 m per second squared, what is the period of the oscillation, and how does it compare with the same tube filled with water?

options.text: The same as for water, because the larger restoring force of the mercury is matched by its larger inertia
Longer than for water by the square root of thirteen and a half, because mercury is denser
options.misconception: believes the density raises the restoring force without raising the inertia

options.text: Shorter than for water by the square root of thirteen and a half, because the mercury is harder to set moving
options.misconception: gets the right density dependence but the wrong direction

options.text: The same as for water to three figures, but the amplitude settles sooner because mercury is more viscous
options.misconception: accepts the right period for the wrong reason, naming a different liquid property

questions.explanation: The oscillation of a liquid column is set by the ratio of the restoring force to the inertia, and the density appears in both. Displacing the liquid by x in one limb raises it by x in the other, so the unbalanced weight is the area of the tube times twice x times the density times the acceleration due to gravity, which is the restoring force, while the inertia is the mass of the whole column, the area times the length times the density. Taking the ratio of inertia to stiffness gives the length divided by twice the acceleration due to gravity, and the density appears in neither the numerator nor the denominator of that ratio once it has been cancelled, so the period is two pi times the square root of the length divided by twice the acceleration due to gravity, 0.898 s here, with no trace of the 1.36e4 kg per cubic metre. Writing it out as an equation of motion makes the cancellation explicit: the column mass is the density times the bore area times the length and the effective stiffness is twice the density times the bore area times the acceleration due to gravity, so their ratio is the length over twice the acceleration due to gravity, and the 1.36e4 and the bore area both cancel. So the first option is right and the second and third are wrong, and the fourth is right about the period but wrong about the reason, since the density does not appear in the period at all.
questions.hint: The restoring force and the inertia both scale with the density, so their ratio does not.

questions.topic: Energy lost per cycle to the damping of an oscillator
questions.learningObjective: express the energy lost per cycle in terms of the quality factor
questions.stem: Carrying a quality factor of 12.0 at an amplitude of 0.1000 m, a mass of 0.200 kg on a spring of spring constant 50.0 N per metre sheds energy steadily to damping. What fraction is lost in each complete cycle, and how much energy in J goes in the first cycle?
questions.explanation: The damping removes energy steadily rather than in one lump, so the fraction lost per cycle has to come from the exponential decay rather than from a single subtraction. The amplitude of a damped oscillator falls as an exponential in the time, and the energy falls as its square, so the energy is multiplied across one period by the exponential of minus two pi divided by the quality factor. The fraction lost is therefore one minus that exponential, which is 0.408 of the energy. The starting energy is the elastic energy at the amplitude, one half of the spring constant times the square of the amplitude, 0.250 J, and the loss in the first cycle is that fraction of it, 0.102 J. Treating the loss as linear in the period rather than exponential gives two pi divided by the quality factor, 0.524, which is a usable shortcut only for a large quality factor and which overstates the loss here, as it must: an exponential always keeps less than a straight line through the same starting point. Even this good quality factor of 12.0 therefore sheds 40.8 per cent of the energy on every swing, and a bell meant to ring for a minute needs a quality factor in the thousands, which is why bells are made of hard alloys and hung freely.
questions.hint: The energy decays exponentially, so the fraction lost per cycle is one minus the exponential of minus two pi over the quality factor.

The ratio of the two stores here is a shade under one, since 0.0600 m is a little beyond the amplitude divided by the square root of two, which is the point at which the two are exactly equal, so the elastic store is already the larger of the two. The general rule is that the stores are equal at a displacement of the amplitude over the square root of two, and that beyond that point the elastic energy is the larger of the two while the speed is on the way down.

The mass is to the right and the acceleration is negative, so the acceleration opposes the displacement, and that opposition is the definition of a restoring force and the reason the motion oscillates at all. questions.topic: Driving above the natural frequency lowers the response
questions.learningObjective: compare a driven response away from resonance with the resonance response
questions.stem: A spring system of mass 0.200 kg and spring constant 50.0 N per metre is driven at 8.00 Hz by a force of amplitude 5.00 N against damping of 2.00 N*s per metre, while its undamped natural frequency is 2.52 Hz. How does the steady-state amplitude at the driving frequency compare with what the same drive would give at the natural frequency, and why?

options.text: The amplitude is smaller away from resonance, because at resonance the spring contributes no opposition at all and only the damping is left to limit the response
The amplitude is larger away from resonance, because the damping is less effective when the drive is out of step
options.misconception: believes the damping weakens when the drive is off frequency

options.text: The amplitude is the same at every driving frequency, because the damping alone sets the response
options.misconception: believes the response is independent of the driving frequency

options.text: The amplitude is larger away from resonance, because the spring adds to the drive when out of step
options.misconception: believes the spring reinforces the drive when they are out of step

questions.explanation: The response of a driven oscillator is set by two competing terms, a stiffness term that opposes the drive when the drive is faster than the natural motion and a damping term that opposes it always. Exactly at the natural frequency the stiffness term vanishes, because the spring is already supplying just the force needed to keep the mass moving at that rate and nothing is left over, so the only thing limiting the amplitude is the damping, and the amplitude there is the driving force divided by the damping constant times the driving angular frequency, 0.158 m. Drive the system away from that frequency and the stiffness term reappears, adding a second opposition in quadrature with the damping, so the amplitude must fall, and at 8.00 Hz it is only 0.0107 m, a factor of 14.7 below the resonance value. This is why a driven system responds most strongly near its natural frequency and why the sharpness of that peak, measured by the quality factor, is the useful figure for characterising a resonator such as a violin string or a radio aerial.
questions.hint: Compare the two terms in the denominator: one vanishes at resonance and both are present away from it.

Working the other way round, taking the length as a half wavelength and solving for the frequency gives the fundamental as the wave speed divided by twice the length, which reproduces 440 Hz and closes the loop. A shorter length of the same string at the same tension therefore raises the fundamental in direct proportion to the shortening, which is why a violinist's finger position changes the pitch.

questions.explanation: The total energy is fixed at the amplitude, one half of the spring constant times the square of the amplitude, 0.250 J, and at the displacement where the two stores are equal each of them must be half of that, 0.125 J. The elastic energy at a displacement x is one half of the spring constant times the square of x, so setting that equal to half the total gives the square of x as the square of the amplitude over two, and the displacement is the amplitude divided by the square root of two, which is 0.0707 m. The same result falls out of the energy partition, since the kinetic energy is the total less the elastic part and the two are equal when the elastic part is half the total, and checking the arithmetic confirms it: one half of 50.0 times 0.00500 is 0.125 J, exactly half of 0.250 J. The general result is worth remembering, because the same displacement of the amplitude over the square root of two appears in the acceleration question, where it is the point of maximum speed, and it is the point at which the speed is the greatest and the restoring force is least.
questions.hint: Each store is half the total energy, and the elastic energy is one half of k times the square of the displacement.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Energy lost to damping over a quarter cycle
questions.learningObjective: compute the energy a damped oscillator loses over part of a cycle
questions.stem: Starting from a turning point, a spring system of mass 0.200 kg and spring constant 50.0 N per metre runs at an amplitude of 0.1000 m while losing energy to a damping force of strength 2.00 N*s per metre. How much energy in J has been lost by the time the mass first reaches the equilibrium position?
questions.explanation: The damping force always opposes the motion, so it removes energy steadily, and the loss over any interval is best found by bookkeeping the total mechanical energy at the two ends. Taking the exact damped motion, the amplitude envelope falls as an exponential at a rate of the damping constant over twice the mass, which is 5.00 per second, and the mass starts from rest at the amplitude, so the energy there is entirely elastic at 0.250 J. Running until the mass first reaches equilibrium, which takes 0.126 s, the total energy there is the kinetic energy alone, and the difference of 0.179 J is what the damping has removed. The same loss is confirmed by a different route, integrating the loss rate over the interval in time: the instantaneous power dissipated is the damping constant times the square of the speed, and integrating that over the quarter cycle gives 0.179 J, the same figure. The size of the result is the useful part, since a loss of 71.7 per cent of the total energy in a single quarter cycle is substantial, which is why this amount of damping would visibly flatten the trace of a measured oscillation, whereas a light damping loses only a small fraction over a whole cycle and leaves the motion looking sinusoidal.
questions.hint: Compare the total mechanical energy at the turning point with that at the equilibrium position, or integrate the loss rate over the interval.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Which changes leave an oscillator period unchanged
questions.learningObjective: identify the changes that do and do not affect an oscillator period
questions.stem: Four statements each describe a change made to a mass on a spring. Put them in order from the change that makes the period shortest to the change that makes it longest, including those that leave it unchanged. Where two changes give the same period, place the second immediately after the first.

options.text: The spring is replaced by one of three times the spring constant, and the mass is left alone
The amplitude of the swing is doubled, with the mass and the spring unchanged
The mass is doubled, with the spring unchanged
The spring is replaced by one of one third the spring constant, and the mass is left alone

questions.explanation: The period of a mass on a spring is two pi times the square root of the mass divided by the spring constant, and the amplitude does not appear in it at all, so the amplitude change and the unchanged case belong together in the middle. A stiffer spring at three times the constant shortens the period by the square root of three, making it the shortest of all, and a spring of one third the constant lengthens the period by the same factor of the square root of three, making it the longest. Doubling the mass sits between them, lengthening the period by the square root of two, which is less than the square root of three, so the ordering runs from the stiff spring through the two unchanged cases to the doubled mass and finally the soft spring. The reason the amplitude is absent is worth stating, because it surprises people: the period of simple harmonic motion is set by how quickly the restoring force grows with displacement, and the size of the swing does not change that, which is the same amplitude-independence that makes a pendulum usable as a clock provided the swing stays small.
questions.hint: The period depends on the mass and the spring constant and not on the amplitude; compare the ratios of their square roots.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Explaining a resonance build-up in terms of energy flow
questions.learningObjective: explain the observed growth of a driven oscillation step by step
questions.stem: A glass is placed on a turntable and a speaker beside it plays a note at a frequency that is slowly raised. Describe, step by step, what happens to the glass as the frequency passes through the value at which the glass itself would ring, and explain the whole sequence in terms of where the energy goes.

answer.exemplar: Far below the natural frequency of the glass, the driving force reverses direction many times while the glass is still moving in the direction it started, so each push arrives against the existing motion and removes energy. The glass therefore rings more quietly than if it were not being driven at all, and the driving force is doing negative work on it. As the driving frequency rises, the glass completes less than one whole swing in the time the drive takes to complete a cycle, and the pushes begin to arrive later in the motion each time, so the net work per cycle becomes less negative. Exactly at the natural frequency, a push arrives each time the glass passes through the same displacement moving in the same direction, so the drive is always in step with the motion and does positive work on every cycle. Energy now flows steadily from the speaker into the glass, and the amplitude grows cycle by cycle, limited only by the damping, which removes energy at a rate that grows with the amplitude. The build-up stops when the average power the drive delivers equals the average power the damping removes, and that balance sets the height of the peak. Above the natural frequency, the drive again arrives out of step, now in advance of the motion rather than behind it, so the net work per cycle becomes negative once more and the amplitude falls. The whole sequence is therefore a small, a peak, and a small again, and the reason the peak is sharp is that the damping is what limits it.

questions.explanation: A driven oscillator is best understood by asking, at each instant, whether the driving force is pushing with the motion or against it, because the work the drive does is positive in the first case and negative in the second. Below the natural frequency the drive completes a cycle while the glass is still completing only a part of its own swing, so the later pushes land against the earlier motion and the net work per cycle is negative, taking energy out of the glass rather than putting it in. As the driving frequency climbs towards the natural frequency, the phase between drive and motion shrinks towards zero, the negative work per cycle shrinks with it, and at resonance the pushes arrive exactly in step with the passage through the equilibrium point, so every cycle delivers positive work and the amplitude grows. The growth is not unlimited because the damping force removes energy at a rate proportional to the speed and therefore to the amplitude, so the amplitude settles where the incoming power matches the outgoing power. Above the natural frequency the drive leads the motion, the net work per cycle is negative again, and the amplitude decays. The peak is sharp precisely because the only thing limiting the build-up is a damping that is small in absolute terms, which is why a lightly damped object such as a wine glass or a bell responds so dramatically at one narrow band of frequencies and hardly at all elsewhere.
questions.hint: Ask at every stage whether the driving force is pushing with the motion or against it, and whether the net work per cycle is positive or negative.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Counting oscillations to measure a frequency
questions.learningObjective: obtain the frequency of an oscillator by counting its swings over a time
questions.stem: A mass of 0.200 kg hangs on a spring of spring constant 50.0 N per metre and is set oscillating. An observer counts 40.0 complete swings in a measured interval of 15.9 s. What frequency in Hz does that give, and what spring constant in N per metre does the measurement imply?
questions.explanation: Counting swings over a measured interval is the standard laboratory method of finding an oscillator's frequency, and the frequency is the count divided by the time, 40.0 cycles in 15.9 s, which is 2.52 Hz. Working from one period instead, the time for a single swing is the measured interval divided by the count, 0.398 s, and taking its reciprocal returns 2.52 Hz, the same figure. The reason the count is made over many swings rather than one is precision, since a hand-timed single swing of a fast oscillator carries a large relative error, while timing several dozen and dividing brings that error down by the same factor. Inverting the period expression gives the spring constant the measurement implies, the mass times the square of the angular frequency, which is 50.0 N per metre, a value that agrees with the 50.0 N per metre stated to the accuracy of the timing, and that comparison is the check that the whole measurement is self-consistent.
questions.hint: Frequency is the count divided by the time, and the spring constant follows from the mass and the angular frequency.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Damping lengthens the period of an oscillation
questions.learningObjective: compute the damped period and compare it with the undamped one
questions.stem: An oscillator of mass 0.200 kg and spring constant 50.0 N per metre is damped with a coefficient of 0.400 N*s per metre. Its undamped period would be 0.397 s. What is the actual period, and by what percentage is it longer than the undamped value?

options.text: 0.397 s, longer by 0.201 per cent, because the damping reduces the restoring force
options.misconception: puts the damping term inside the square root with a plus sign, which would shorten the period

options.text: 0.397 s, unchanged, because the damping only removes energy and does not affect the timing
options.misconception: believes damping changes the amplitude but not the period

options.text: 0.398 s, longer by 0.201 per cent, because the damping reduces the restoring force the mass effectively feels
0.397 s, shorter by 0.200 per cent, because the damping makes the mass effectively lighter
options.misconception: believes damping speeds the oscillation, as though the mass had been reduced

questions.explanation: Damping enters the equation of motion as a term proportional to the velocity, and when the steady oscillation is substituted into the equation that term acts like a reduction in the effective restoring force, so the oscillation runs slightly slower than it otherwise would. The damped angular frequency is the square root of the square of the undamped angular frequency less a quarter of the square of the damping constant divided by the mass, which here is 15.8 rad per second less the 1.000 per second damping rate, giving 15.8 rad per second and a period of 0.398 s. Comparing with the undamped period of 0.397 s, the ratio is the reciprocal of the square root of one minus the damping ratio squared, 1.00, so the period is longer by 0.201 per cent. The first option is right and the second is the mirror-image error, since a plus sign in that place would shorten the period, which is the wrong direction for a force that opposes the motion. The third and fourth options are the two common misunderstandings, one that damping leaves the timing alone and one that it makes the mass effectively lighter, neither of which survives the fact that the damping force always points backwards.
questions.hint: The damping term reduces the effective restoring force, so the period lengthens slightly.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Worked procedure for reading a speed off an oscillation
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of a speed measurement from an oscillation
questions.stem: Four statements describe how the speed of a mass on a spring is found at a stated displacement during its oscillation. Put them in the order in which they occur, earliest first.

options.text: The speed at the stated displacement is obtained from the square root of the spring constant times the square of the amplitude less the square of the displacement, all divided by the mass
The amplitude of the oscillation is read from the largest displacement reached
The spring constant and the mass of the oscillator are measured independently
The mass-spring system is set oscillating and held at the stated displacement, so the instant of interest is well defined

questions.explanation: The order here follows the logic of the dependency, since the final step uses the amplitude, the spring constant and the mass, so all three have to be in hand before it. Measuring the spring constant and the mass comes first and is independent of the oscillation, and it is done separately because both are properties of the system rather than of its motion. Setting the system oscillating and identifying the instant comes next, because the speed is only well defined at a particular displacement and the experimenter has to be sure the mass is passing through that displacement on the way in rather than on the way out, though the speed happens to be the same on both passes. Reading the amplitude comes third, since the amplitude is the largest displacement reached and is what the final expression needs, and it is best read by watching where the mass turns round rather than by timing. The calculation is last, and the expression used is the one obtained by subtracting the elastic energy at that displacement from the total energy of the oscillation, or equivalently by the sinusoidal form of the speed, and the two agree because both are statements of the same energy conservation.
questions.hint: Everything the final formula needs must be measured first: the constants, then the state of the motion, then the amplitude.
